newsitem.title: USA: California electric utility rate cut bonds debated.
newsitem.headline: California electric utility rate cut bonds debated.

text.p: Formal debate over terms for debt securities aimed at financing a 10 percent electricity rate cut for residential and small business customers in California will begin next week at the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) in San Francisco.
But stakeholders have already begun to lay out their positions on the rate reduction bonds, which will also lower the carrying costs on a portion of investor-owned utilities' uneconomic costs.
Costs such as nuclear power plant investments and above-market power purchase contracts deemed likely to be unprofitable under market competition are estimated to total up to $30 billion.
Earlier this month, California's three major utilities asked the CPUC to approve plans to issue up to $7.3 billion of the new securities.

PG&E Corp's Pacific Gas & Electric Co applied to issue up to $3.5 bilion in bonds, while Edison International's Southern Calfiornia Edison Co asked to issue up to $3.0 billion and Enova Corp's plans to issue up to $800 million in the new securities.
Each of the utilities said they intend to use net proceeds to reduce their capitalization, with the cuts roughly equal to current debt and equity ratios.
The new securities were authorized under electric industry restructuring legislation passed in California last year.

But The Utility Reform Network (TURN), the state's largest utility consumer advocacy group, said Tuesday it questions whether the bonds would be in the best interests of residents and small businesses.
In a formal protest filed with the CPUC, TURN said the bonds would lock ratepayers into a 7.5 percent long-term debt for at least ten years.

"To get one dollar of present value benefit, residential ratepayers will be forced to pay off a debt of between $9 and $11, including principal and interest," said TURN executive director Nettie Hoge in a statement.
TURN maintained that California consumers are entitled, under the state legislation, to a 10 percent rate cut regardless of any bond financing.
The consumer group also warned that the debt cannot be pre-paid and could result in rate increases if utility requests to adjust for errors in energy use forecasts are allowed.
